cards.title: The Research Station
cards.body: Three samples. Three states. One substance. Tonight we find out why matter looks so different depending on how it's arranged.

cards.title: Your Role
cards.body: You're Dr. Adaobi's Junior Research Assistant. You'll control the experiments and read the results.

cards.title: How to Play
cards.body: Drag the wall to give particles more or less room. Watch what changes.

missions.title: The Three States
missions.learningGoal: Observe how particle spacing and motion change between solid, liquid, and gas states by dragging the container wall.

payload.missionContext: Something arrived at the lab tonight that needs identifying. Three samples — same substance, three different containers. We don't know which state each one is in yet. I'm going to show you how we find out.

guidedSteps.narration: Look — the particles barely move. They vibrate right where they are. That's what being a solid means at this scale: every particle is locked in by its neighbours, pulling on each other so strongly that nobody goes anywhere.
guidedSteps.instruction: Watch the particles in the solid state.

guidedSteps.narration: Feel that? Tap two particles close together to test the bond. That pull between them — that's why a solid holds its shape. Break that and you've got a liquid.
Now they can slide. Same particles, same substance — just more room between them. They're still attracted to each other, but not strongly enough to stay in one place. That's a liquid.
See the difference? They drift apart instead of snapping back hard. Still some pull — that's why liquids stay together in a pool instead of flying off in all directions.
guidedSteps.instruction: Tap two particles again — test the bond in liquid.

guidedSteps.narration: And now they're free. Same particles — just too far apart to feel each other's pull anymore. They go wherever they can reach.
guidedSteps.instruction: Keep dragging the wall — all the way out.

guidedSteps.narration: Nothing pulls them back. The particles are too far apart to feel each other's attraction. That's the defining feature of a gas — that's also why gas fills every container you put it in.
guidedSteps.instruction: Tap two particles one last time.

missions.title: Shape, Volume, and Space
missions.learningGoal: Connect particle spacing to observable properties: fixed shape, fixed volume, and compressibility.

payload.missionContext: Same idea — different substance. This time we're looking at what the three states mean in terms of shape and volume. Watch what happens to the arrangement as you drag.

guidedSteps.narration: In the solid state, every particle is fixed in position. The substance has a definite shape and a definite volume — it doesn't matter which container you put it in, it keeps its shape.
Now liquid. The particles slide — so the substance takes the shape of whatever container holds it. But the volume? That stays the same. You can't squeeze a liquid smaller than its particles allow.
guidedSteps.instruction: Drag the wall to the liquid zone.

guidedSteps.narration: And gas. No fixed shape, no fixed volume — it fills every bit of space available. Try to squeeze it into a smaller container and it pushes back harder. The particles just spread further apart when given room, or collide with the walls more when compressed.
guidedSteps.instruction: Drag the wall all the way out to gas.

guidedSteps.narration: Now pull it back to solid. Watch the particles return to their grid. Same particles — same number — just arranged differently. The three states aren't three different substances. They're three different arrangements of the same one.
guidedSteps.instruction: Drag the wall back to the solid zone.

missions.title: Read the Sample
missions.learningGoal: Identify the state of a substance from its particle behaviour — without being told what state it is.

payload.missionContext: An unlabelled sample arrived this evening. Dr. Adaobi needs you to identify its state from the particle behaviour alone. No labels. No hints. Just what you can see.
